AI is a pretty controversial topic, but let's be honest, in today's day and age, knowing how to use it properly is becoming a critical skill. From time to time, people ask me how to use AI for research. Well, for starters, avoid the ways you should definitely not use AI. And this is a prime example. Whether Oliver prepared it himself or an assistant did it for him, either way, a terrible job was done. And ultimately, he was the one delivering the speech. So how should you use AI properly? Rule number one, actually read what AI provided to you before you deliver it. But if we're talking seriously, ideally, before you even start, you should already have at least a basic understanding of what you are researching or writing about. Then you can use AI as a knowledgeable friend who can help you. Not as an all-knowing oracle, and definitely not as a replacement for your own brain. It can help you structure your argument, spot weak points, explain difficult material, and show you counter-arguments you may have missed. AI can also help you find sources, but your prompt matters enormously. A common mistake is to first decide what you want to believe and then ask, find new studies proving this. Congratulations, you have basically asked a very advanced search engine to help you with your confirmation bias. Instead, ask for the strongest evidence both supporting and opposing your claim. Ask what the scientific consensus is, where researchers disagree, what important context is missing, and what evidence would prove your idea wrong. Your goal should be to get closer to the truth, not to recruit AI into pushing your agenda. Then check the sources yourself. Make sure the study actually exists and look at what it really says, the sample, the methods, the limitations, and the actual conclusion. A paper mentioning your topic does not automatically support your claim, and AI can sometimes describe a study much more confidently than the researchers themselves did. Cross-running the claim through other AIs can also be useful, but again, be careful with that too. Different models can sometimes repeat the same mistake. The ideal verification is opening the original study or dataset yourself and checking it directly. You should also ask AI to clearly separate established facts from interpretations and speculation, and to tell you when it is uncertain. If you wrote the script yourself, ask AI to double-check it. If AI helped you writing it, double-check it yourself. And then, before publishing anything, check it once again to be sure. And yes, sometimes the evidence will oppose your own views. In that case, you may need to change those views. That should be a good day, because it means you learned something and went against your own prejudices. But in the case of the video in the beginning, the problem is not that a politician used AI. The problem is that, apparently, nobody used enough human intelligence after it.
